en: Striking; catching attention
hook: ARRESTING: it ARRESTS your attention — you can't move on.
story: Arresting. Rafi walked through the art exhibition at Shilpakala Academy, glancing at painting after painting without slowing down. Then he stopped. A huge canvas showed an old boatman's face, wet with rain, his eyes staring straight at the viewer. Rafi stood there for ten minutes. The painting was arresting: so striking that it seized his attention and held it. Think of a policeman arresting someone: an arresting image stops you in your tracks. Synonyms: striking, eye-catching, riveting.

gre.s: Although the exhibition as a whole was forgettable, one ____ portrait of a fisherman's weathered face held visitors in front of it for minutes at a time.
gre.clue: held visitors in front of it for minutes at a time

en: To scold or criticize severely
hook: CHASTISE: CHASE them with words until they're CHASTE (corrected).
story: Chastise. Tanvir came home at two in the morning after a friend's wedding, without calling anyone. His father was waiting in the drawing room. For twenty minutes he chastised Tanvir: how careless, how selfish, how worried his mother had been. Tanvir stared at the floor and said nothing. To chastise is to scold or criticize severely. It shares a root with chaste and chasten, from a Latin word meaning to make pure, as if the scolding cleans out the fault. Synonyms: rebuke, reprimand, castigate.

gre.s: Far from praising the minister's handling of the flood, the committee's report went out of its way to ____ him for delays that had cost lives.
gre.clue: Far from praising

en: Difficult to handle because of size, weight, or complexity
hook: CUMBERSOME: ENCUMBERS you, weighing you down.
story: Cumbersome. Nadia's family was moving from Chittagong to Dhaka, and the hardest item was her grandmother's old wooden almirah. It was enormous, heavy, and impossible to turn on the narrow stairs. Four men struggled with it for an hour. Cumbersome means difficult to handle because of size, weight, or complexity. The word also fits rules and systems: a cumbersome visa process with twelve forms and four offices is just as hard to carry. Synonyms: unwieldy, clunky, awkward.

gre.s: The old registration process was so ____, requiring eleven separate forms and three office visits, that many applicants simply abandoned it halfway through.
gre.clue: requiring eleven separate forms and three office visits

en: Careful management of resources; thrift and efficiency in use
hook: GRE trick: ECONOMY of words means using no more words than needed.
story: Economy. Every month Sara's mother received a small salary, yet the family never went short. She bought vegetables in season, used cooking oil carefully, and turned leftover rice into breakfast. Her neighbours admired her economy: careful management of resources, wasting nothing. On the GRE, economy often describes style, too. A writer with economy of language never uses ten words when three will do. So economy means thrift and efficiency, not only a nation's finances. Synonyms: thrift, frugality, efficiency.

gre.s: Her prose is admired for its remarkable ____: she never uses three words where one will do, and every sentence seems to earn its place.
gre.clue: she never uses three words where one will do

en: Basic; relating to the simplest beginning stages
hook: ELEMENTARY: the basic ELEMENTS.
story: Elementary. On the first day of the GRE quant course, Arif felt almost insulted. The teacher began with fractions, percentages, and the area of a triangle, things he had learned in class six. But the teacher explained that elementary ideas are the foundation for everything harder. Elementary means basic, relating to the simplest beginning stages. An elementary school teaches the first steps of learning, and an elementary mistake is one even a beginner should avoid. Synonyms: basic, rudimentary, fundamental.

gre.s: Although the textbook advertises itself as an advanced treatment of the subject, its exercises are so ____ that a first-year student could finish them in an afternoon.
gre.clue: a first-year student could finish them in an afternoon

en: To decorate; to add details, often untrue, to make a story more interesting
hook: EMBELLISH: add BELLS to it, decorate.
story: Embellish. Every time Kamal told the story of the snake in his village pond, it grew. First it was a small water snake. A year later it was six feet long. By the time he told it at the hostel, it was a cobra that had chased him up a coconut tree. Kamal embellished the story: he added exciting details that were not true. To embellish also means to decorate, like embellishing a sari with embroidery. Synonyms: embroider, exaggerate, adorn.

gre.s: The journalist was dismissed when editors discovered her habit of choosing to ____ her reports with vivid quotations that no source had ever actually spoken.
gre.clue: vivid quotations that no source had ever actually spoken

en: Feeling intense happiness and excitement
hook: EUPHORIC: feeling EU-phoria, extreme 'yay!'
story: Euphoric. Late at night, Bangladesh won a cricket match in the very last over against one of the strongest teams in the world. Within minutes, the streets around Dhaka University filled with students shouting, singing, waving flags, and hugging strangers. Nobody could sleep. The whole city felt euphoric: intensely happy and excited. The noun is euphoria. Euphoria is more than contentment; it is a rush of joy, often brief. Its opposite is despair. Synonyms: elated, ecstatic, jubilant.

gre.s: The mood among investors was ____ on the day the merger was announced, but within a week the celebration had given way to anxiety as share prices collapsed.
gre.clue: the celebration had given way to anxiety

en: To officially clear someone from blame
hook: EX-ONERATE: remove the ONUS (burden) of guilt.
story: Exonerate. A cashier at a Gulshan bank was accused of stealing two lakh taka. For weeks, colleagues whispered about her. Then the security camera footage was finally reviewed. It showed a different employee taking the money. The bank's inquiry exonerated her: it officially cleared her of all blame. Ex means off, and onus means burden: to exonerate is to take the burden of guilt off someone. Its opposite is incriminate. Synonyms: clear, absolve, vindicate.

gre.s: The new DNA evidence did more than cast doubt on his conviction; it served to ____ him entirely, and the court ordered his release that same afternoon.
gre.clue: the court ordered his release that same afternoon

en: To estimate unknown values by extending known trends
hook: EXTRA-POLATE: extend the line EXTRA far beyond the data.
story: Extrapolate. Zayan had been tracking his GRE practice scores: three hundred in March, three hundred and five in April, three hundred and ten in May. He drew a straight line on graph paper and extended it. 'By August I will score three twenty-five,' he announced. He was extrapolating: estimating unknown values by extending a known trend. His teacher warned that progress rarely stays a straight line. Extra means outside: you extrapolate beyond the data you actually have. Synonyms: project, infer.

gre.s: Since reliable gauge records existed only up to 1990, the analysts had to ____ from earlier trends to estimate how high the river might be rising today.
gre.clue: Since reliable gauge records existed only up to 1990

en: To lose strength or momentum; to hesitate
hook: FALTER: like a FAULT in your step.
story: Falter. Joya had practised her debate speech twenty times. She began confidently, but halfway through, she glanced at the judges, saw one of them frowning, and lost her place. Her voice faltered. She paused, stammered, and searched her notes. To falter is to lose strength or momentum, or to hesitate. Economies falter, engines falter, and courage falters. Think of a fault in a machine making it falter and stall. Synonyms: waver, stumble, flag.

gre.s: The runner led for most of the marathon, but in the final kilometre her legs began to ____, and two rivals swept past her before the finish line.
gre.clue: two rivals swept past her

en: Having or showing intense passion
hook: FERVENT: burning with FERVOR.
story: Fervent. Every evening during the election season, Babu's uncle stood at the village tea stall, arguing passionately for his candidate. He printed posters with his own money, walked miles to rallies, and could recite every campaign promise from memory. He was a fervent supporter: full of intense passion. Fervent comes from a Latin word meaning to boil, the same root as fervour. A fervent prayer is one said with burning sincerity. Synonyms: ardent, zealous, passionate.

gre.s: Though once a ____ supporter of the policy, attending every rally and writing letters to every newspaper, he became its harshest critic after seeing its effects.
gre.clue: attending every rally and writing letters to every newspaper

en: To stir up trouble or rebellion
hook: FOMENT: FERMENT trouble, let it bubble.
story: Foment. During a dispute at a garment factory, a few outsiders began spreading false rumours that the owners were about to cut everyone's wages. They held secret meetings and handed out angry leaflets. Within days, workers were blocking the gates. The outsiders had fomented unrest: they deliberately stirred it up. To foment is to stir up trouble or rebellion. Picture someone stirring a pot until it boils over. Synonyms: incite, instigate, provoke. Its opposite is quell.

gre.s: Officials accused the pamphleteers of trying to ____ unrest among the factory workers, though the workers insisted their anger needed no outside encouragement.
gre.clue: their anger needed no outside encouragement

en: An embarrassing social mistake
hook: GAFFE: a GAFFE makes everyone LAUGH at you.
story: Gaffe. At his first office party, Shuvo met a tall woman by the snack table and complained loudly about the new managing director, who, he said, was strict and boring. The woman smiled politely and said, 'I am the new managing director.' Shuvo wanted to disappear. It was a terrible gaffe: an embarrassing social mistake. Politicians are famous for gaffes, like forgetting the name of the town they are visiting. Synonyms: blunder, faux pas, slip.

gre.s: The ambassador's ____ was mocked for weeks: at a state dinner, he raised his glass to the host country using the name of its bitter rival.
gre.clue: he raised his glass to the host country using the name of its bitter rival

en: Not conforming to accepted or orthodox beliefs
hook: HETERO-DOX: DIFFERENT belief (orthodox = correct belief).
story: Heterodox. In a university economics seminar, every student repeated the standard textbook view. Then Ishita stood up and argued that the whole model ignored how real villages share risk through family networks. Some professors frowned; a few were intrigued. Her views were heterodox: not conforming to accepted beliefs. Hetero means other, and dox means opinion, as in orthodox, meaning right opinion. So heterodox means holding a different opinion. Synonyms: unorthodox, dissenting, nonconformist.

gre.s: Her ____ views on monetary policy, which rejected nearly every assumption of mainstream economics, made her unpopular with central bankers but fascinating to her students.
gre.clue: rejected nearly every assumption of mainstream economics

en: Overly theatrical or dramatic in behavior
hook: HISTRIONIC: like a HISTORIC actor overacting.
story: Histrionic. When an opponent barely brushed his shoulder, the football player threw himself to the ground, clutched his leg, rolled over three times, and raised his arms to the sky as if he had been shot. Moments later he was sprinting happily. His reaction was histrionic: overly theatrical and dramatic. Histrio was the Latin word for an actor, so histrionic behaviour is acting in real life. Synonyms: melodramatic, theatrical, overwrought.

gre.s: The defence lawyer's ____ outbursts, complete with tearful pleas and pounding fists, struck the jury as calculated theatre rather than genuine emotion.
gre.clue: calculated theatre rather than genuine emotion

en: Implied though not directly expressed; absolute and unquestioning
hook: IMPLICIT: IMPLIED. Opposite: EXPLICIT.
story: Implicit. Lamia's mother never said, 'Do not come home late.' But every time Lamia returned after dark, her mother sat silently at the dining table, looking at the clock. The message was implicit: implied, though never directly expressed. Implicit is the opposite of explicit, which means clearly stated. A second sense means absolute and unquestioning, as in implicit trust: deep down, Lamia trusted her mother implicitly. Synonyms: implied, unspoken, tacit.

gre.s: Although the contract never states it outright, both parties share the ____ understanding that the tenant will maintain the garden in exchange for lower rent.
gre.clue: never states it outright

en: Free from injury or violation; untouched
hook: IN-VIOLATE: NOT VIOLATED.
story: Inviolate. In one village near Sylhet, there is a small forest beside an old shrine. For generations, nobody has cut a single tree there, hunted a bird, or even carried away fallen branches. The villagers believe the grove is sacred. It has remained inviolate: free from injury or violation, completely untouched. In means not, so inviolate means not violated. A promise or a principle can also be inviolate. Synonyms: untouched, intact, sacrosanct.

gre.s: For centuries the sacred grove remained ____: villagers believed that anyone who cut even a single branch would bring disaster on the whole community.
gre.clue: anyone who cut even a single branch would bring disaster

en: Something that puts one at a disadvantage; legal responsibility
hook: LIABILITY: something you're LIABLE for, a burden.
story: Liability. Farhan was the fastest bowler on his university team, but he also argued with umpires in almost every match. Twice the team was penalised, and once they nearly lost a final because he was suspended. The captain finally told him, 'Your temper is a liability.' A liability is something that puts you at a disadvantage. In law and accounting, liability also means legal responsibility, or a debt. Its opposite is an asset. Synonyms: burden, handicap, drawback.

gre.s: His reckless remarks to the press, once dismissed as charming, had become a serious ____ for the campaign, costing it the support of several key donors.
gre.clue: costing it the support of several key donors

en: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion
hook: OBSTINATE: an OBSTACLE that won't move.
story: Obstinate. Rahim's grandfather refused to take his blood pressure medicine. The doctor explained the risks, his children begged, and his grandchildren hid the sweets. Still he insisted that he had never been sick in seventy years and needed no pills. He was obstinate: stubbornly refusing to change his opinion. Obstinate often suggests unreasonable stubbornness. Hear the word obstacle in it: an obstinate person stands in your way like a rock. Synonyms: stubborn, intransigent, mulish.

gre.s: Despite overwhelming evidence that the bridge design was flawed, the chief engineer remained ____, refusing even to open the inspectors' report.
gre.clue: refusing even to open the inspectors' report

en: Done with or employing great care and thoroughness
hook: PAINS-TAKING: TAKING great PAINS.
story: Painstaking. Tania, a conservator at a Dhaka museum, was restoring a two-hundred-year-old manuscript. Using a tiny brush and a magnifying lens, she cleaned each page, mended each tear with special tissue, and checked each letter against old photographs. One page took her a whole week. Her work was painstaking: done with great care and thoroughness. The word literally means taking pains. Synonyms: meticulous, thorough, scrupulous. Its opposites are careless and slapdash.

gre.s: The restoration was ____: over eleven years, a small team of conservators cleaned the enormous mural one square centimetre at a time.
gre.clue: one square centimetre at a time

en: Calm and unemotional; not easily excited
hook: PHLEGMATIC: slow and calm, like thick PHLEGM.
story: Phlegmatic. The cyclone signal rose to number ten, and the coastal shelter was in panic. Children cried and men shouted over each other. Old Abdul the boatman simply sat in a corner, sharing out puffed rice and calmly telling families where to put their things. He was phlegmatic: calm and unemotional, not easily excited. Ancient doctors believed that too much phlegm in the body made a person sluggish and calm. Synonyms: imperturbable, stolid, unflappable.

gre.s: While the other passengers screamed as the plane lurched through the storm, the ____ pilot calmly announced that they would still land on schedule.
gre.clue: calmly announced

en: Remarkably impressive in size, extent, or degree
hook: PRODIGIOUS: like a PRODIGY, extraordinary.
story: Prodigious. At the book fair, Mahin's little cousin amazed everyone. She had read over four hundred books by the age of eleven and could recite long poems by Rabindranath Tagore from memory. Her appetite for reading was prodigious: remarkably impressive in size and degree. The word is related to prodigy, a child with exceptional talent. A prodigious amount of rain, or prodigious energy, means an enormous amount. Synonyms: enormous, colossal, phenomenal.

gre.s: Mozart's output was ____: although he died at only thirty-five, he had already composed more than six hundred works.
gre.clue: more than six hundred works

en: A natural tendency to behave in a particular way
hook: PROPENSITY: a PRONE tendency.
story: Propensity. Sabbir had one strange habit. Whenever he was nervous, he bought snacks. Before every exam, every job interview, and every family wedding, his pockets filled with chanachur and biscuits. His friends teased him about his propensity to stress-eat: his natural tendency to behave that way. Pro means forward and pend means hang, as in pendulum: a propensity is the way you naturally lean. We speak of a propensity for violence or for risk. Synonyms: tendency, inclination, penchant.

gre.s: Given his well-known ____ to exaggerate, his colleagues learned to divide every figure he quoted by at least two.
gre.clue: his colleagues learned to divide every figure he quoted by at least two

en: A feeling of doubt or unease, especially about one's conduct
hook: QUALM: a small QUALITY check of your conscience.
story: Qualm. Anika found a wallet near the Mirpur bus stand containing ten thousand taka. Her rent was overdue, and for a moment she thought of keeping the money. But the student card inside showed a young girl's face, and Anika felt a qualm: a sudden uneasy feeling that keeping it would be wrong. She returned it. A qualm is a feeling of doubt or unease, especially about one's conduct. Ruthless people have no qualms. Synonyms: misgiving, scruple, pang.

gre.s: She felt not the slightest ____ about reporting her own manager to the auditors, since she had watched him falsify the accounts with her own eyes.
gre.clue: since she had watched him falsify the accounts with her own eyes

en: To go back on a promise or agreement
hook: RENEGE: RE-NEG(ATE) your promise.
story: Renege. Before the election, a candidate promised Imran's village a new bridge. He shook hands with the elders and even laid a foundation stone. After winning, he announced that the money would go to a highway instead. He had reneged on his promise: gone back on it. Renege is almost always followed by on. Hear the word negative inside it: reneging is saying no to what you once said yes to. Synonyms: backtrack, default, go back.

gre.s: Having promised in writing to fund the new library, the company later tried to ____ on the deal, claiming the agreement had never been binding.
gre.clue: claiming the agreement had never been binding

en: Ungenerous; restricting in amount
hook: STINTING: giving only a tiny STINT.
story: Stinting. Rumana's landlord was famously stinting. He allowed the water pump to run only one hour a day, fixed nothing until it broke completely, and gave the night guard a bonus of one hundred taka at Eid. Stinting means ungenerous, restricting the amount given. The word appears most often in its opposite form: unstinting praise means generous, wholehearted praise. To stint on something is to give too little of it. Synonyms: stingy, miserly, tight-fisted.

gre.s: Critics accused the government of being ____ with flood relief: families that had lost everything received barely a week's rations.
gre.clue: received barely a week's rations

en: To moderate or soften the intensity of something
hook: GRE trick: to TEMPER is to TONE DOWN, like tempering spicy food with yogurt.
story: Temper. Priya wrote a furious online review of a restaurant that had served her cold biryani. Before posting it, she read it again and decided it was too harsh. She removed the insults, mentioned the friendly waiter, and tempered her criticism: she moderated and softened it. As a verb, to temper is to moderate. Blacksmiths temper steel, heating and cooling it so it is less brittle. Losing your temper is the opposite of tempering anything. Synonyms: moderate, soften, mitigate.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the committee's harsh conclusions, the chair added a paragraph acknowledging the team's genuine achievements under difficult conditions.
gre.clue: acknowledging the team's genuine achievements

en: Not certain or fixed; hesitant
hook: TENTATIVE: like a TENT, temporary, not permanent.
story: Tentative. Nadia's friends were planning a weekend trip to Cox's Bazar. 'Let us say Friday morning,' said Rafi, 'but nothing is final until we know the bus tickets are available.' They wrote the plan in pencil. It was tentative: not certain or fixed. Tentative can also describe a manner, as in a tentative smile or tentative first steps, meaning hesitant. It comes from a Latin word meaning to try: a tentative plan is only a trial. Synonyms: provisional, hesitant.

gre.s: The two governments reached only a ____ agreement, one that both sides stressed could be revised or even abandoned after further talks.
gre.clue: could be revised or even abandoned after further talks

en: Never done or known before
hook: UN-PRECEDENT-ED: no PRECEDENT, never happened before.
story: Unprecedented. In 2022, floodwater in parts of Sylhet rose higher than anyone could remember. Elders who had lived through decades of monsoons said they had never seen anything like it. Newspapers called the flood unprecedented: never done or known before. A precedent is an earlier example that guides later decisions, so unprecedented means having no earlier example at all. Lawyers search for precedents; an unprecedented case has none. Synonyms: unparalleled, unheard of, novel.

gre.s: The flood was truly ____: in two hundred years of written records, the river had never risen even half as high.
gre.clue: had never risen even half as high

en: Lively and full of energy, especially in personality
hook: VIVACIOUS: full of VIVA (life).
story: Vivacious. When Mitu joined the office, the quiet accounts department changed overnight. She greeted everyone by name, told funny stories at lunch, organised a birthday party for the tea boy, and laughed so warmly that even the grumpy manager smiled. Colleagues called her vivacious: lively and full of energy. Viv means life, as in vivid and revive. A vivacious person seems more alive than everyone else in the room. Synonyms: lively, bubbly, spirited.

gre.s: Unlike her reserved older sister, Shathi was ____, filling every room with laughter and chatter from the moment she arrived.
gre.clue: Unlike her reserved older sister
